**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Reconstruct the outline behind somebody else's paper, build your own the same way — topic sentence by topic sentence — and defend your research problem in front of the room.

## Session A · 2:05–3:15

Academic writing I — the method. A paper is built outline first: one topic sentence per paragraph, in order, before any prose exists. We start backwards, taking a published paper apart into the outline that must have produced it — which is also this week's exercise, and the fastest way to see that good writing has a skeleton. Then forwards: outline, then sketch, then full text. Every written product in this course is submitted in those stages, so the argument is fixed before the sentences are. Then what a problem statement in particular has to do — scope, unit, population, and the 'so what' in the first sentence rather than the fourth paragraph — and the failure modes: the topic with no question, hedging, the buried claim, the review that reviews without arguing

## Session B · 3:35–4:30

Every session B opens with a ten-minute team stand-up: what you did,
what is blocked, and who does what next — in writing, submitted with
the session output.

Milestone 1: each team presents its research problem in five minutes and takes questions from the room — the feedback you get here is what you write up this week. Then the first peer evaluation
